To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
evolving morphology and control of a robot such that it exhibits conservative behavior indirectly selects appropriate modularity, thus increasing its evolvability.

(1) the morphology of an embodied agent can facilitate the evolution of a modular controller, (2), this controller can enable the agent to correctly recognize a composition of familiar sensory inputs as a novel environment, and (3), the ability to do so is increased if the morphology and controller are evolved together and if fitness selects for conservative behavior.

(1) the morphology of an embodied agent influences the ability of evolution to find useful and modulated controllers, (2) a modular controller enables different parts of a body to sense and act independently, (3) this can enable the agent to recognize a novel situation as composed of familiar percepts, and (4) this can enable it to respond appropriately without further evolution.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to evolve embodied systems that can adapt to novel environments, which is an important problem in the field of artificial life and evolutionary robotics.
understanding how to design evolutionary algorithms that are capable of evolving complex, modular and evolvable controllers for embodied agents.
the question of how the morphological and neural structure of an agent influences the evolvability of its behavior, and what the relationship is between modularity and evolvability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evolution of morphologies that are able to sense and act in different parts of the environment, in addition to the evolution of controllers that are able to use these parts in a modular way, is a prerequisite for the evolution of evolvable robots.
the evolution of morphology, in addition to selection for robust and conservative behavior, is a key factor in the emergence of modularity and evolvability in embodied agents.
the morphology of a robot is an essential part of its control system and, in fact, its controller is a part of the robot's morphology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
morphological and neural modularity can be co-evolved to enable the evolution of robust and evolvable robots.
morphological evolution can be a key factor in the evolution of neural modularity and evolvability in embodied systems.
we demonstrate that a combination of morphological and behavioral evolution is necessary for the evolution of modularity in embodied agents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of morphologies can increase evolv- ability of the evolved controllers by enabling them to exhibit more robust behavior in a wider range of environments.
modularity in embodied agents can be selected for by an evolutionary algorithm without the explicit selection of modularity, and that this can be achieved by evolving both morphology and control.

the morphologies of robots should be allowed to evolve along with their controllers, and that fitness functions should be designed to select for conservative behaviors, as this will increase the likelihood that a robot will exhibit appropriate modularity.
